Periodic mandate re-grounding helped conservative agents in low-signal markets but worsened outcomes for aggressive agents, indicating that effective long-term deployment of autonomous financial agents requires selective, mandate-aware adjustments tailored to agent profiles and market conditions.

item.title: Researchers evaluate large language models for cross-lingual relation extraction on Romanian, finding fine-tuned QLoRA improves F1 by 22 points but smaller encoders perform competitively [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have explored cross-lingual relation extraction (RE) for Romanian by translating an English benchmark dataset and evaluating large language models (LLMs) alongside smaller encoder models. They tested the Gemma 4 31B model in zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings using QLoRA, comparing its performance to four encoder baselines including Romanian BERT and XLM-RoBERTa variants. Fine-tuning with QLoRA significantly improved F1 scores by over 22 points and narrowed the performance gap between English and Romanian. The study found that while the large 31B parameter model achieved the highest scores, smaller encoder models with 125M to 560M parameters performed competitively, often within a few points of the fine-tuned LLM. This suggests that for Romanian RE tasks, smaller models may offer a more practical balance of performance and computational efficiency. The researchers have made the translated dataset, evaluation code, and trained models publicly available to support further work in low-resource language processing.

item.title: Researchers find vision-language models overpredict shared understanding in asymmetric dialogue by conflating map content with established common ground [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have found that vision-language models (VLMs) tend to overestimate shared understanding in collaborative dialogues by confusing the presence of shared map content with actual established common ground between participants. Their study, based on 13,077 annotated reference expressions from HCRC MapTask dialogues, shows that while authentic map images improve model performance, they also cause models to over-predict alignment, treating potential shared information as if it were mutually understood. The research involved controlled experiments manipulating dialogue context and map information access, revealing that this bias arises from task-relevant map content rather than the visual presentation itself. Models often rely on static referential cues instead of tracking how mutual understanding develops through dialogue history. This pattern was most evident in the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model and observed to varying degrees in other architectures, indicating a common challenge in accurately modeling grounding in asymmetric dialogue.

item.title: Researchers present CHERRY, a compute-efficient language model training approach combining selective supervision, depth compression with recurrent recovery, and fusion of compressed experts on a 1.8B-parameter Korean model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced CHERRY, a novel approach to training compute-efficient language models demonstrated on a 1.8 billion-parameter Korean model. The method combines three techniques: selective supervision focusing on the 15% of tokens carrying semantic content, depth compression with recurrent recovery to reduce model layers while maintaining performance, and fusion of compressed experts through a Mixture of Efficient Experts (MoEE) to enhance prediction accuracy. These techniques collectively improve training efficiency and model performance while reducing computational requirements. Selective Ground Truth Token Training (SGT) concentrates learning on key tokens, achieving a 4.5-fold increase in per-supervised-token efficiency and recovering about 67% of the full-sequence loss reduction from limited supervision. Depth compression reduces a 48-layer transformer to 6 layers, restored via recurrent unrolling to match the performance of larger dense models with fewer parameters. Combining multiple compressed models as experts further improves results beyond individual models. The researchers validate these methods on the CHERRY-1.8B Korean foundation model, emphasizing the scope and limitations of their findings based on one model family and loss-based metrics.

item.title: Researchers propose a parameter-neutral transformer feed-forward layer using explicit fuzzy logic and self-forgetting quantifiers to improve grammatical licensing detection and interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a parameter-neutral replacement for the feed-forward sublayer in transformers, using explicit fuzzy logic operations and self-forgetting quantifiers to enhance grammatical licensing detection and interpretability. This negation-capable feed-forward network (NC-FFN) applies fuzzy set operations on sigmoid-bounded memberships, achieving competitive performance with traditional models while providing explicit logical forms for each unit. The approach addresses limitations in grammatical licensing and quantifier handling by introducing sequence quantifiers with learned forgetting rates, improving model legibility and performance on language tasks such as LAMBADA. The new model demonstrates that grammatical licensing detectors emerge naturally within the feed-forward layers, with units responding to licensors like comparatives and negative-polarity items and carrying memory forward to predict licensed words. This interpretable mechanism offers insight into how feed-forward layers represent and license grammatical structures, resulting in a transformer model that maintains language-model quality while enhancing transparency and understanding of its internal computations.

item.title: Researchers present first systematic evaluation of data referencing errors in large language models on tables and propose a 4B-parameter critic model improving accuracy by up to 12% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have conducted the first systematic evaluation of data referencing errors (DREs) in large language models (LLMs) when processing tables, revealing that these errors occur across models ranging from 1.7 billion to 20 billion parameters. These errors involve incorrectly citing or omitting table values, which undermines the accuracy and reliability of intermediate reasoning steps despite the models' understanding of table structures. The study introduces a 4-billion-parameter critic model that improves answer accuracy by up to 12% through critic-based filtering and rejection sampling. The critic model achieves an average F1 score of 78.2% in detecting both in-distribution and out-of-distribution DREs, effectively assisting larger models during inference. This approach highlights the importance of addressing data referencing errors to enhance the correctness of LLM outputs on tabular tasks and offers a promising method for improving model reliability in handling structured data.

item.title: Researchers propose reinforcement learning with metacognitive feedback to improve uncertainty calibration and self-assessment in large language models, achieving up to 63% better performance than standard RL [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced a new approach called reinforcement learning with metacognitive feedback (RLMF) to improve large language models' (LLMs) ability to accurately assess and express their own uncertainty. This method enhances models' metacognitive skills, addressing issues like overconfidence in hallucinations and poor recognition of knowledge limits, by refining completion rankings based on the quality of the model's self-judgments and selecting valuable training data. Applied to the task of faithful calibration, RLMF achieved up to 63% better performance than standard reinforcement learning while maintaining accuracy across diverse tasks. The approach involves a two-stage process: first calibrating the faithfulness of the models' self-reported confidence scores, then translating these into natural, context-sensitive expressions of uncertainty through targeted output editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RLMF not only improves uncertainty calibration but also enhances the models' ability to monitor and regulate their cognitive processes, positioning it as a promising paradigm for advancing LLM metacognition and alignment. By leveraging metacognitive performance as a reinforcement learning signal, this method overcomes limitations of previous intrinsic feedback techniques, potentially leading to more trustworthy and reliable AI systems capable of better self-assessment and adaptive behavior.

item.title: Researchers propose ASR-agnostic multimodal spectrotemporal model using Mel spectrograms for early dementia detection, achieving up to 93.7% accuracy on Slovak and Spanish datasets with cross-lingual stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed an ASR-agnostic multimodal model that uses Mel spectrograms to detect early signs of dementia with high accuracy. The model extracts spectrotemporal displacement fields from consecutive spectrogram frames to capture shifting spectral energy patterns as biomarkers of cognitive decline. It combines these features with acoustic embeddings through a cross-attention mechanism and aggregates them using a Transformer encoder, achieving up to 93.7% accuracy on Slovak and Spanish datasets while showing cross-lingual stability. The study trained independent models on English, Slovak, and Spanish speech corpora, each involving clinical protocols targeting cognitive domains related to daily living activities. Results showed varying performance across languages, with the Slovak model outperforming others and the English baseline affected by known recording artifacts. Ablation studies highlighted that the benefit of multimodal fusion depends on the dataset, being crucial when signals are distributed across modalities but less effective or unnecessary when one modality dominates or signals are weak. These findings suggest that the proposed approach offers a language-independent framework for early dementia detection using speech, with implications for developing non-invasive cognitive assessment tools adaptable to different languages and recording conditions.
